title: The Left–Right Spectrum
hook: "Left" and "right" are political shorthand the whole world uses — but they began as nothing more than which side of a room people sat on.
key_points: The terms come from seating in the 1789 French National Assembly: reformers left, traditionalists right.
Broadly, 'left' favors greater equality and change; 'right' favors tradition, order, and established hierarchy.
It's a rough simplification — a single line can't capture every issue or position.
Analysts often add a second axis (e.g. social liberty vs authority) for a fuller map.
content_html: Few pieces of political vocabulary travel as widely as "left" and "right," yet their origin is almost accidental. In the French National Assembly of 1789, deputies who favored revolutionary change and challenging the old order happened to sit on the president's left, while those defending the monarchy and tradition sat on the right. The seating chart became a metaphor, and the metaphor outlived the assembly to become a near-universal way of locating political positions.
extra_html: As a rough guide, the left came to stand for greater equality, social reform, and a more active role for collective action in correcting injustice, while the right came to stand for tradition, order, established hierarchy, and caution about rapid change. Encyclopaedia Britannica stresses that this is a broad generalization, not a precise rule: the specific content of "left" and "right" shifts across countries and eras, and many positions don't fit neatly on one line at all. That is why analysts frequently add a second axis — for instance, plotting economic views against social ones, or liberty against authority — so that someone can be economically left but socially conservative, or the reverse. The spectrum remains useful precisely because it is simple, but its simplicity is also its main limitation.

related.title: Major Political Ideologies
related.hook: An ideology is a worldview about how society should be run — and a handful of them frame most political arguments you'll ever hear.

related.title: Political Parties & Party Systems
related.hook: Parties are how scattered voters become an organized choice. Whether a country has two big ones or a dozen shapes how its whole politics feels.

related.title: What Democracy Means
related.hook: Rule by the people: a system where political power ultimately traces back to citizens, usually through regular, free elections.

flashcards.prompt: Where do the political terms 'left' and 'right' come from?
flashcards.back_html: The seating of the 1789 French National Assembly — reformers sat on the left, supporters of the old order on the right.

flashcards.prompt: In broad terms, what does the 'left' tend to favor compared with the 'right'?

choices.text: Greater equality and change, versus tradition, order, and established hierarchy
Lower voter turnout, versus higher voter turnout

flashcards.explanation_html: As a rough generalization, the left emphasizes equality and reform and the right emphasizes tradition, order, and existing hierarchies.

flashcards.prompt: Why do analysts often add a second axis to the left–right line?

choices.text: A single line oversimplifies — a second axis (e.g. liberty vs authority) captures more
Because left and right mean exactly the same thing
To make the spectrum impossible to use

flashcards.explanation_html: One line can't capture every position, so a second dimension is added to map, for example, social freedom against state authority.
